title: Widest Ramp Between Two Values
statement:
You get an integer array nums. A ramp is a pair of indexes i < j with nums[i] ≤ nums[j]: the right end is at least as high as the left end. Its width is j − i.

Return the width of the widest ramp, or 0 if there is none.

examples.why: The 1 at index 1 and the 1 at index 6 form a ramp of width 5. Equal values count.
Every value is lower than everything before it, so no pair works.
The smallest value, 0 at index 2, only reaches width 1. The best left end is the 1 at index 0, which pairs with the 4 at index 3.

hints: Fix the right end j. Which left ends are worth considering at all?

If some earlier index already has a value ≤ nums[i], then i is never the best left end: that earlier index is further left and at least as low. The useful left ends form a strictly decreasing sequence from the start.

Push those candidates on a stack in one left-to-right pass. Then scan j from the right: while the stack top's value ≤ nums[j], record j − top and pop it, since no later (smaller) j can do better for it.

explain.intuition:
A left end i is only worth trying if nothing before it is as low: otherwise the earlier, lower index beats it for every j. So the useful left ends are the running minima from the left, a strictly decreasing sequence of values. One pass collects them on a stack.

Now walk j from the right end towards the left. For the candidate on top of the stack (the lowest so far, the one furthest right), the first j you meet with nums[j] ≥ its value is the widest partner it will ever get, because every later j is further left. So record the width and pop it, then test the next candidate against the same j. Each index is pushed and popped at most once.
steps: Left to right: push index i onto the stack when the stack is empty or nums[i] is smaller than the value at the top.
Right to left over j: while the stack is not empty and nums[top] ≤ nums[j], update best = max(best, j − top) and pop.
Stop early if the stack becomes empty.
pitfalls: Pairing the global minimum with the last larger value. In [1, 5, 0, 4] the minimum gives 1, but the answer is 3.
Using a strict < in the pop test. Equal values form a valid ramp: [0, 0] has width 1.
Popping candidates in the first pass like a normal monotonic stack. Here the first pass only pushes; the pops happen during the right-to-left scan.

solutions.title: Try every pair
solutions.idea: For each left end, scan from the far right and stop at the first value that is high enough.

solutions.title: Sort indexes by value
solutions.idea: Visit indexes in order of value (ties by index). Every index seen earlier is a valid left end, so the best ramp ending here uses the smallest index seen so far.

solutions.title: Decreasing stack of left ends
solutions.idea: Collect the running minima as candidate left ends, then sweep right ends from the back and pop every candidate that is satisfied.

followups: Require nums[i] < nums[j] strictly. Which comparisons change?
Values stream in from the right end one at a time. Can you keep the widest ramp so far up to date?
